title: Voting Experts Feared “Chaos” on Election Day. So Far, It Hasn’t Materialized.
author: Peter Elkind
content:
As Americans cast ballots on Tuesday, voting experts’ deepest concerns largely
didn’t materialize on a mostly routine Election Day.

Tuesday’s relative quiet followed an anxious run-up in which the Trump
administration pressed forward with unprecedented efforts to assert more
federal control over elections.

Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has
tried to [force states to turn over their unredacted voter
rolls](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-doj-voter-data-lawsuits/) and to
[restrict mail-in voting](https://www.propublica.org/article/trumps-plan-to-
restrict-mail-voting). The Department of Homeland Security has [used its
resources](https://www.propublica.org/article/save-voter-citizenship-tool-
mistakes-confusion) to [identify and prosecute noncitizen
voters](https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-
security-investigations), an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s
massive crackdown on immigrants.

The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that
American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the
scales in favor of Democrats.

* * *

### Help Us Report on Key Election Issues

ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what
isn’t. We’re monitoring **voter suppression** and interference, **election
observers** and**** poll watchers, **extremism** tied to the election,
and**ICE activity** at the polls. Have you seen something?

[Send Us a Tip](https://www.propublica.org/tips/)

* * *

Courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans, but Trump and his top
deputies have kept up the pressure. In the days before the midterm, they
threatened to prosecute election officials who didn’t reject ballots from
people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens.

The administration didn’t explicitly rule out sending federal agents to the
polls or seizing ballots or voting machines.

Election experts told ProPublica the cumulative effect of these steps was to
ramp up anxiety about the vote and to erode voters’ trust in the system.

“The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a
lot of doubt,” said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the
bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he
worried that this would make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.”

In an emailed response to questions before Election Day, a DHS spokesperson
said Immigration and Customs Enforcement was “not planning operations
targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people
at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven
targeted enforcement.”

### “Paper Trail” Podcast

Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “[Paper
Trail](https://www.propublica.org/series/paper-trail).”

The DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying,
prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S.
citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American
elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the
consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.”

Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to
mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans said they’d
expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm.

Republicans said they would focus on issues such as voter eligibility and
voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National
Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats planned to
concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, said Angelo
Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson.

Here are five issues that voting rights experts said they were watching in
this year’s election:

![An election worker in an orange vest leans on an umbrella next to signs for
ballot drop-offs as voters walk along a tree-lined pathway toward a polling
site.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261030-election-day-expectations-
florida.jpg?w=752)People arrive to vote early on Oct. 27 in Coral Gables,
Florida. Lynne Sladky/AP Images

### 1\. Will There Be Federal Interference?

As clocks hit 5 p.m. on the East Coast, there’d been no confirmed reports
about federal law enforcement at the polls. Homeland Security Secretary
Markwayne Mullin [told reporters at the White
House](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/03/us/midterms-2026-election-day-
trump/eee0c811-cf73-5a14-900c-eeaed5477c08?smid=url-share) that he hadn’t sent
immigration agents to the polls.  

Still, an incident during early voting in Leon County, in the Florida
Panhandle, illustrates how widespread such fears have been.

Mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was
“furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked
outside the county’s busiest voting location last month, after he’d been
repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this.

He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were
headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The
[episode](https://www.thedailybeast.com/donald-trumps-border-goons-spotted-at-
blue-citys-polling-site) generated a
[flurry](https://www.tallahassee.com/story/news/politics/elections/2026/10/21/federal-
agents-at-florida-voting-site-prompt-fbi-complaint/92372347007) of
[news](https://news.wfsu.org/wfsu-local-news/2026-10-25/border-agents-looking-
to-vote-raised-concerns-at-a-tallahassee-polling-site)
[coverage](https://www.cbsnews.com/miami/news/south-florida-border-patrol-
agents-early-voting-north-florida/).

“Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it
shows pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,”
Earley said.

It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places.

Nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state
officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond
if, indeed, there were real federal interference. The group has “war-gamed”
how to react if government agents attempted to commandeer voting equipment or
ballots.

“We’ve seen the tension and chaos that’s in the air,” Brown said. He called
the federal government “the biggest challenge to smooth elections right now,
which is not the way it’s supposed to be.”

A DOJ spokesperson said “the best preparation for any election official is
following federal law.”

As is routine in federal elections, DOJ monitors were watching over polling
places Tuesday. The agency had assured states that its observers would follow
the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. In Michigan,
the state attorney general’s office said it received reports of monitors
requesting training materials in Dearborn. A similar report came in about
monitors’ interaction with election workers in Flint. The DOJ team overseeing
Michigan later told state officials that this was inconsistent with the
training they received.

Similarly, in New Mexico, the secretary of state’s office received reports of
Justice Department monitors “asking some unusual questions and questioning
voters" in Bernalillo County, a spokesperson told ProPublica, adding that the
office later received reassurance from the Justice Department that “it would
be addressed.”

This issue also surfaced in August during the primary election in Wyoming,
where [poll workers reported feeling
uneasy](https://apnews.com/article/wyoming-primary-justice-department-
monitors-gordon-3d454cdb2834025b3b82364888f226d0) when DOJ monitors asked
about their training and to inspect voting systems. The state’s governor
criticized these actions as “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.”

![Election workers process and sort ballots at numbered tables in a large room
cordoned off by a sign reading “restricted area,” “authorized personnel only”
and “Orange County Registrar of Voters.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261030-election-day-expectations-
california.jpg?w=752)Workers prepare ballots to be scanned for counting in
Orange County, California, on Oct. 28. Apu Gomes/Getty Images

### 2\. What Effect Will Noncitizen Voter Challenges Have?

The Trump administration’s multipronged effort targeting alleged noncitizen
voters has [already led to eligible voters being improperly
removed](https://www.propublica.org/article/save-voter-citizenship-tool-
mistakes-confusion) from the rolls. Voting rights groups feared this would
block some U.S. citizens from being able to vote when they showed up Tuesday,
but it’s not yet clear whether this happened.

Federal officials have made clear they plan to go after anyone they think is
committing voter fraud.

On the first day of early voting in Texas, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for
the Southern District of Texas, [posted a YouTube
video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9hEG3q8tKFA) announcing his intentions.
“If you violate federal election law,” he warned, “I will hunt you down and
prosecute you.”

This threat came days after the DOJ sued California, seeking to block the
state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are
“likely” noncitizens. [The administration had obtained the state’s public
voter
rolls](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cacd.1043513/gov.uscourts.cacd.1043513.62.3.pdf),
which the DHS had blended with its own immigration information and third-party
data.

[In a court
filing](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28856214-california-response-
doj-lawsuit/), California called the claim that there are 20,000 noncitizens
on its voter rolls “specious.” [Los Angeles
County](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cacd.1043513/gov.uscourts.cacd.1043513.32.1_2.pdf)
analyzed a sampling of the likely noncitizen voters that the federal
government claimed were registered there. Many weren’t registered in the
county or had never voted, the analysis showed. Some said on their voter
registration forms that they were born in the United States.

Asked about the case, the DOJ told ProPublica, “Federal law prohibits
noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and the Department has a duty to
enforce it.”

After lower courts [rejected the DOJ’s motion for an emergency
order](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cacd.1043513/gov.uscourts.cacd.1043513.149.0.pdf)
that would have barred California from counting the 20,000 voters’ ballots,
the U.S. Supreme Court declined the Trump administration’s request to
intervene in the dispute. On Thursday, the administration also sent grand jury
subpoenas to California officials demanding records about their response to
allegations of noncitizens on the state’s rolls. Late Friday, a federal judge
issued a restraining order blocking those DOJ demands, calling them an
“intimidation plan” that would interfere with legal voting.

Last week, the DOJ [wrote a
letter](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28856231-list-redacted-ltr-to-
steve-hobs-re-non-cit-ballots-102626-1/) threatening to sue Washington state
if officials there refused to review a list of 400 voters it believes to be
noncitizens within 24 hours. [U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told
reporters late last month](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Hw8TXmELL2A) that
the department was considering additional actions, saying there were “a number
of states that we’re looking at.”

In [a letter responding to the DOJ](https://www.sos.wa.gov/about-
office/news/2026/washington-secretary-state-steve-hobbs-response-doj-letter-
about-voter-rolls), Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs called the
government list of 400 names “not reliable,” saying it included U.S. citizens,
people who aren’t registered to vote and duplicate entries. “Time and time
again,” Hobbs wrote, “DHS claims about noncitizen voter registration turn out
to be greatly exaggerated or false.”

Sam Trepel is Rule of Law program director at States United Democracy Center
and a former attorney for the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division. She said the
agency’s actions involving California and Washington were a “disturbing use of
prosecutorial authority.”

Trepel worried that the DOJ would try to seize ballots cast by voters
identified as likely noncitizens, before or after the election, which would
“put their votes at risk and undermine trust more broadly.”

Voting rights advocates also were concerned that the government’s efforts to
target noncitizen voters could frighten eligible voters to the point that they
wouldn’t show up.

[A federal
judge](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.479338/gov.uscourts.cand.479338.87.0.pdf)
recently put limits on [a multistate effort by the DHS to go door-to-
door](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/judge-dhs-noncitizen-voters-ruling/) in
search of suspected noncitizen voters, at least through Election Day, saying
it was illegally intimidating legal voters.

“A voter could say, ‘Well, maybe I don’t want to put myself on the target list
here, maybe I won’t register, or maybe I won’t vote,’” said David Janovsky,
acting director of The Constitution Project at the watchdog group Project on
Government Oversight.

![Tablets with text on their screens that reads “Travis County Clerk’s
Office,” “Elections Division,” “Travis County, Texas” and “start” are lined up
in rows.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261030-election-day-expectations-
texas.jpg?w=752)Equipment for early voting is prepared at the Travis County
Clerk’s Office in Austin, Texas, on Oct. 14. Jay Janner/The Austin American-
Statesman via Getty Images

### 3\. Will There Be Problems at the Polls?

By late afternoon, voters and election officials had reported an array of
delays and ballot-scanning problems.

That includes in New York, where [the State Board of Elections said a
programming
error](https://x.com/NYSBOE/status/2117677659610128512?a=AvAeiyXCx-
ugI2umHI0&s=20) in Westchester County made it impossible to scan ballots using
on-site machines, causing voter concern. Officials have said that all ballots
would be counted.

States often change laws and rules related to voting.

Since 2024, Republican-led states have taken a number of steps that [experts
say](https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/state-voting-
laws-roundup-october-2026) will make it more difficult for some of their
residents to cast ballots and have them count.

A North Carolina law, for example, required voters to provide proof of
identification when sending mail-in ballots. Under new rules, ballots now come
with two envelopes, both of which must be sealed. Ballot rejections had
skyrocketed, [Democracy Docket](https://www.democracydocket.com/news-
alerts/gop-backed-ballot-rules-plague-north-carolina-voters-in-democratic-
stronghold/) reported, because voters weren’t sealing the inner envelope.

[Texas and other states](https://sg.news.yahoo.com/gop-states-made-harder-
vote-090044008.html) cut back on the number and location of polling places,
especially in areas favoring Democrats. [In hotly contested Tarrant
County](https://amp.star-telegram.com/news/politics-
government/article317074374.html), which includes Fort Worth, the number of
polling sites was slashed by almost a third. This prompted fears of long lines
and voter confusion on Election Day. But seven of the 10 voting sites a
reporter visited had waits of less than 15 minutes, and the three with longer
lines were each within a couple of miles of a site with a short wait. In
Tarrant, like many Texas counties, voters can cast a ballot at any location.

Voting rights groups such as the Texas Civil Rights Project are tracking two
issues involving the state’s voter registration systems. A software [error at
the Texas Department of Public
Safety](https://www.votebeat.org/texas/2026/09/23/dps-error-backlogged-voter-
registration-applications-county-election-officials/) stopped several hundred
thousand new voter registrations from being forwarded to local election
officials, preventing them from being added to the rolls. A [separate state
system](https://www.votebeat.org/texas/2026/10/16/voter-registration-records-
address-update-backlog-secretary-of-state/) for updating registration
information wasn’t processing changes for several weeks, leading to more
backlogs.

Texas Civil Rights Project attorney Sarah Chen said the group received more
complaints than usual from voters this Election Day who said they had to cast
provisional ballots because registrations had not been processed. How much of
a jump is unclear, Chen said, because counties have six days to report
provisional ballots.

Every election features some issues with voting equipment.

During early voting, there were isolated complaints involving touch-screen
voting machines — including one from Dolly Parton’s sister in Tennessee —
spawning fears that machines had been “rigged” to switch votes.

ES&S, the company that makes the machines garnering the complaints, told
ProPublica that the company hadn’t received widespread reports. Election
experts say occasional problems with touch-screen machines don’t signify
tampering or manipulation. Any attempt to tamper with programming would
surface during testing by election officials and be corrected, they said.

![A United States Postal Inspection Service poster pinned to a board titled
“letter and package bomb indicators.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261030-election-day-expectations-threats.jpg?w=752)A
poster at the King County elections headquarters in Washington. Last month,
officials in several states, including Arizona, received envelopes with an
unknown white powder. Arizona eventually deemed the material nontoxic, but
Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said “the fear it caused was real.” David
Ryder/Getty Images

### 4\. How Secure Will the Election Be?

Incidents in the run-up to the midterms had ratcheted up election officials’
concerns about the potential for both cyber and physical attacks.

On Tuesday, bomb threats were made at polling places in at least two states,
Ohio and Michigan. In Ohio, [a threat at a Toledo elementary
school](https://www.wtol.com/article/news/local/vote/police-investigate-
school-threat-in-lake-township-sweep-tps-polling-
location/512-97755e13-a45e-4b5b-9d45-4fc9e015776e?utm_medium=social&utm_source=facebook_WTOL_11&fbclid=IwY2xjawVXSaxleHRuA2FlbQIxMABwZG9mBWJyaWQRMVpIdWM3VjBuQnVyT3lmcExzcnRjBmFwcF9pZBAyMjIwMzkxNzg4MjAwODkyAAEfaOWtzOWsfi8eHdOVG3D3irHBP3f6FOz8_yMmJCvuraCmKx0MO1_IYKnMDzM_aem_TMt9ER4r2Mc4ckYfRToF_g)
caused the polling place to be evacuated, but the site was later cleared and
voting resumed. In Michigan, the threat involved a polling place in Gibraltar,
and an investigation similarly determined the threat was unfounded, according
to the Michigan Department of State.

Last month, officials in several states, including Arizona, received envelopes
with an unknown white powder. Arizona eventually deemed the material nontoxic,
but Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said “the fear it caused was real.”

In 2024, false bomb threats, thought to be from foreign actors, caused
widespread evacuations of vote-counting sites across the country. The
disruptions were brief, however, in part because a message board funded by the
federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, alerted
election officials that the FBI had deemed the threats not credible.

Trump, however, has dismantled CISA since retaking the presidency, leaving
states and local election officials to grapple with both physical and cyber
threats on their own. [Election](https://www.cisecurity.org/)
[nonprofits](https://securingelections.org/) have stepped up to try to fill
the gap, and states, with CISA’s help, have enhanced their own cyber defenses.

Derek Tisler, counsel and manager for the elections and government program at
the Brennan Center for Justice, said the federal government’s absence has
weakened the defenses.

“States acting on their own just do not have the same power,” he said.

![A woman holding papers walks past a bear statue along a marble hallway, with
signs reading “vote” and “voting” on the wall.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261030-election-day-expectations-alaska.jpg?w=752)A
voter at a polling site in Anchorage, Alaska, on Oct. 27. The Justice
Department has sued the state, seeking to block it from certifying the result
of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent doesn’t win. The suit claims
the system is unfairly rigged against Sen. Dan Sullivan, because another
Alaska man named Dan Sullivan also qualified for the general election ballot.
Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images

### 5\. Where Will Postelection Challenges Come From?

Election lawyers [fear that actions](https://slate.com/news-and-
politics/2026/10/2026-midterm-news-doj-alaska-trump-
fraud.html?gift_token=eTi6jUaJRB2os0SnVj_-uA) by the Trump administration in
the run-up to the midterms suggest the government will aggressively pursue
postelection challenges if the results are not to the president’s liking.

Late last month, the DOJ sued Alaska, seeking to block the state from
certifying the result of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent doesn’t
win. A federal judge [threw out that
lawsuit](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/01/nx-s1-6023766/doj-alaska-lawsuit-
senate-race-dan-sullivan) on Sunday, but the administration is expected to
appeal.

Trump has said [he personally
ordered](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/-WMBP2_Maic) the lawsuit to be filed.
It claims the system is unfairly rigged against Sen. Dan Sullivan, because
another Alaska man named Dan Sullivan also qualified for the general election
ballot. [The New York Times reported last
week](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/28/us/politics/alaska-dan-sullivan-
conspiracy-peltola.html) that campaign aides to Democratic Senate nominee Mary
Peltola orchestrated the candidacy of the second Dan Sullivan after a
monthslong, statewide search to recruit someone with the same name. (The
Justice Department has also reportedly [sent 20 letters to
Democrats](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/03/justice-department-
letters-peltola-sullivan-alaska-senate-race), including a prominent elections
lawyer who has represented Peltola and other candidates, warning that they
might be targets of criminal investigations.)

Nonetheless, the DOJ’s case is unusual, both because [federal law
prohibits](https://www.justice.gov/jm/jm-9-85000-protection-government-
integrity#9-85.300) the government from interfering with an active election
and because challenges typically come after voting is complete. Postelection
challenges are most often brought by losing candidates in state courts.

“This is using the federal government to interfere with our election process
in a way that I think is pretty troubling on multiple levels,” said Brown, the
Washington attorney general.

In response to ProPublica’s questions, the DOJ pointed to [Blanche’s statement
about the lawsuit on social
media](https://x.com/AGToddBlanche/status/2114072424815776119?s=20), which
said the agency “does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop
the certification of Alaska’s election.” (The lawsuit calls it “vital” that
the state not certify “any election result that may be impacted by voter
confusion” and asks the judge to prevent Alaska from doing this.)

Some election lawyers have suggested that if the GOP suffers significant
losses, Trump could try to pressure Republicans in Congress to block new
members from being seated. Several lawyers, including [Derek Muller, a law
professor at the University of Notre
Dame](https://electionlawblog.org/2026/fearmongering-about-stealing-congress-
on-january-3-2027/), say that the incoming Democratic majority would be able
to fend off such an effort; courts, too, are likely to stymie it, though it
might cause a short delay, according to Muller.

Brown said he and other attorneys general are also planning how to respond if
local election officials or boards refuse to certify election results, based
on their own claims of fraud or claims by the administration.

“I worry tremendously about what they might do,” Brown said.
